t: Models now write proofs that machines verify.
This October, Lean checked two AI-claimed refutations of the Exponential
Time Hypothesis, an age-old and seemingly impossible problem.
Verification also already guards real systems.
CompCert, a proven C compiler, is qualified for avionics,
and seL4 kept a red team from taking over a helicopter in flight.
But verification ends where software ends.
In biosafety and biosecurity, foot-and-mouth virus most likely
escaped England's labs through long-damaged drains.
In aerospace engineering, an acoustic test shook loose fasteners
on Webb's sunshield, part of a 29-month delay.
In mechanical and product design, Dyson built over 5,000
prototypes before the first Dyson vacuum succeeded.
Most products are still tested by hand.
So we built RAAV, Robot as a Verifier.
RAAV tests a physical prototype against its manual and specification
with a low-cost robot arm and reports what it measured.
Vision language action models like SmolVLA and NVIDIA's GR00T N1
learn new tasks from demonstrations and grade themselves,
but RAAV chooses an alternative architecture to split the work.
System 1 handles what must be exact, fast, and safe.
Perception, inverse kinematics, control, force limits,
and verdicts from sensor readings by fixed rules.
System 2, a frontier model, handles what needs context and judgment.
Reading the manual and spec, reasoning over plans of testing, recovering
from failed steps, and diagnosing causes and proposing CAD fixes.
Each does what it's good at, and both benefit from long lines of existing
work and are immune to the classical failures of VLAs, which include
failure to binding and failure for few-shot learning.
Here's revision A of our centrifuge with its manual.
System 1 surveys, scans, segments, maps, and touches the panel.
A fail scan reports back, and System 2 reruns it.
System 2 plans from the manual, and a person approves.
System 1 runs each step of the plan under a 15-newton cap, retries small
misses within its autonomy setting, and judges by fixed rules.
When the first flip hits 16 newtons, it stopped first, resuming took a person.
When the display contradicted the manual, System 2 amended
the plan, and code, not the model, rated the change.
Then, we encounter the lid.
Its thin fin needs a pinch the spec forbids, so System 1 refuses,
and System 2 reports it rather than just guessing.
System 2 traces this to the handle and drafts a hooked
lip, code checks it, and a person approves.
This unmasks a tight well.
The tube sits high, so START shows TUBE.
Rev B fixes both.
The same tests rerun, and it only counts if the score rises.
Our model has never seen this centrifuge before, and this is just the start.
Another arm could sit behind the same model setup.
Plans can come from any manual and we can use any prototype,
and we take extra care to maintain a thoughtful human in the loop.
As AI starts designing hardware, we think every design should
be measured this way before anyone relies on it.
RAAV.
Robot as a Verifier.
